Investors searching for exposure to mission-critical software and hardware often compare Axon Enterprise (NASDAQ:AXON) and Palantir Technologies (NASDAQ:PLTR). Both companies leverage sophisticated technology to solve complex problems for large institutions.

Axon specializes in public safety tools and cloud evidence management for law enforcement. Palantir provides massive data integration and artificial intelligence infrastructure for government and corporate clients. As both companies expand their digital platforms, determining which is the more attractive buy requires a look at their recent financial performance.

The case for Axon Enterprise

Axon Enterprise provides a comprehensive ecosystem of hardware and software designed for law enforcement and public safety professionals. Its product line includes Taser devices, body-worn cameras, and the Axon Evidence platform, which allows agencies to manage digital records securely. The company is actively expanding its presence among defense stocks and international markets across Europe and Asia. No single customer represented more than 10% of total net sales in 2025, which provides a diversified revenue base.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached about $3.4 billion, indicating a 33.6% increase compared to the prior period. This growth was accompanied by a net income of approximately $258.5 million. The company continues to transition customers toward subscription-based software services, which typically offer higher visibility into future sales. This steady growth suggests strong demand for its integrated safety solutions among federal and local agencies.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is roughly 0.6x. This ratio measures total debt relative to shareholder equity, showing how much the company relies on borrowed funds. The current ratio, which compares short-term assets to short-term liabilities, is approximately 2.5x. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow was around $75.1 million. Note that stock-based compensation represented roughly 300% of operating cash flow, meaning reported cash generation is heavily inflated by this non-cash add-back.

The case for Palantir Technologies

Palantir Technologies develops platforms that integrate and analyze massive data sets to help organizations make better decisions. Its customer base is divided between government agencies and commercial enterprises, with a total of 954 customers as of late 2025. The company recently reported a remaining deal value of nearly $11.2 billion, split between its public and private sector contracts. Note that the top three customers accounted for roughly 16% of revenue in 2025. Customer concentration among these top clients adds a layer of risk to the business.

Palantir Technologies has the highest price-to-earnings ratio in a group of five large technology companies. That ratio, the P/E, is what buyers pay for each dollar of a year's profit. Palantir also has the fastest sales growth in the same group. So is the stock priced for what the business delivers?

How does Palantir's price compare with what it delivers?

Our read is that the price matches Palantir's growth, not its profit margin. Microsoft shows this most clearly. Its operating margin, the share of sales left after running costs, is 47.1%. Palantir's is 45.6%, almost the same.

Yet buyers pay 25.6 times profit for Microsoft and 104.5 times for Palantir. Palantir's net income is above its operating income. So part of the profit behind that P/E came from outside its main business.

The gap pays for growth. Palantir's sales rose 87.1% over its latest four quarters. Microsoft's rose 17.9%. Every other company in the group has both a lower P/E and slower growth.

The share price has not kept up. Palantir returned 2.3% over the past year, dividends included, against 12% for the S&P 500. In the month to Monday it fell 19%, even after an 11.1% jump on Monday itself.

Palantir shares fell 19% in a month, and the company sends holders no cash while they wait. If your savings have to cover your bills, a drop like that is hard to sit through with nothing coming in. Palantir Technologies (NASDAQ:PLTR) Chief Technology Officer Shyam Sankar sold 300,000 Class A shares for approximately $47.96 million on Nov. 19, according to a regulatory filing.

The transaction involved shares priced between $153.30 and $167.08.

Before the sale, Sankar converted 300,000 Class B shares into Class A stock on a one-for-one basis. The filing showed that he retained 857,616 Class A shares and 2,943,918 Class B shares through direct ownership after completing the transaction.

Sankar also reported indirect ownership of 599,899 Class A shares held through the Sankar Irrevocable Remainder Trust, where he serves as co-trustee. He disclaimed beneficial ownership of those shares except to the extent of any pecuniary interest.

The scheduled nature of the transaction means the sale was not necessarily a response to recent movements in Palantir's share price.
